title: Longing for union (IV.13)
hookLine: the soul longs to be one with Christ in the sacrament
tomorrow: thirty days in one little book. which line will you keep?

lines: A DINNER ON A VIDEO CALL.
cards: A holiday dinner on a video call. You can see the table, hear the forks and the laughing, and you can't pass the salt. What do you do when you can't get to the table?
Catholics who can't receive communion, because they're sick, or far away, or not able to receive, have an old answer.
They make a spiritual communion: they tell Christ they long for him, and ask him to come into the heart.

teach.h: IS WANTING GOD A WAY OF BEING NEAR?
teach.b: The question underneath is old: is wanting God already a way of being near him? Chapter thirteen of book four answers with pure longing.
Who will grant me, the disciple asks, to find you alone, to open my whole heart to you, and talk as a friend talks with a friend?

teach.h: VERILY THOU ART A HIDDEN GOD.
teach.b: He borrows Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Verily thou art a hidden God." Near in the sacrament, and hidden, so the longing grows instead of fading. He asks to be set on fire and made one spirit with Christ.
That's union in this book: closeness so deep the words run out. Now a neighbor who knows this ache.

The psalms belong first to the Hebrew Bible, and Psalm 42 in the Jewish numbering says it like this, in the Douay-Rheims, where it's Psalm 41: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God."
In the Jewish Publication Society's translation, the next line asks when the psalmist will come and appear before God. Jews and Catholics both pray this psalm, a thirst for the living God.
And one honest difference: in book four, the longing is for Christ, present in the sacrament, a belief Jewish tradition doesn't hold.
Same thirst, read in two houses.
Here's the thing to say at dinner tonight: some of the same words of longing are prayed in a synagogue and a church.

how: Catholics who cannot receive communion, at home, in hospital or watching Mass from afar, can make a spiritual communion, telling Christ of their desire to receive him; Jews and Christians both pray the psalms, including Psalm 42.

o: the heart's wish to be one with Christ
a wedding vow spoken at a nuptial Mass
a monk's promise to live in one monastery

p: longing told to Christ when you can't receive
Isaiah's words, borrowed in book four

s: a spiritual communion only counts if a priest is there
it's a longing told to Christ by someone who can't receive, wherever they are.
Psalm 42 belongs to the Hebrew Bible, and Catholics pray it too
as the hart panteth after the fountains of water, so my soul panteth after thee, O God.
Jews and Catholics read Psalm 42 as the same communion
they share the thirst; the longing for Christ in the sacrament is Catholic belief, not Jewish.

games.q: your Jewish friend says the line about the deer and the water is her favorite psalm. you've heard it at your parish. what's the honest thing to say?
o: we pray the same psalm, the same thirst, and we each read it in our own house.
it's the same prayer, so it means exactly the same thing for both of us.
it's really a Christian psalm about communion that Jews also borrowed.
games.why: the psalm is from the Hebrew Bible first. the thirst for God is shared; the Catholic longing for Christ in the sacrament is an honest difference.

practice: Close your eyes and let one wanting be there without pushing it into a feeling: a person you miss, a place you can't get to, or God. Breathe slowly and stay near the wanting itself.
Catholics who pray may make a spiritual communion here, in their own words.

wordCard.voice: Longing for union. Book four's wish to be one with Christ in the sacrament: near, hidden, and wanted with the whole heart.

orig.note: Latin, Isaiah 45:15 in the Vulgate: verily thou art a hidden God, the line book four borrows.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: one with him, and the longing itself is part of the closeness. Go gently.
